title: Brute Force: Password Cracking
summary: Password cracking attacks the credential material itself rather than the login service. Once an adversary obtains password hashes, for example through credential dumping on a host or from a configuration repository holding network device secrets, they try to recover the plaintext behind them. This work normally happens on adversary owned hardware, away from the victim network, so it produces no authentication failures in your logs and no traffic to your systems. Attackers use dictionaries seeded with real passwords from breaches, mangling rules that add digits or change letters, and precomputed tables that trade storage for speed, with hash type and length deciding the cost. The recovered plaintext may then be reused on systems where pass the hash is not an option, and reused credentials give the attack reach beyond the machine it started on. Defensively the leverage sits at the earlier step: detecting the dumping or repository access that produced the hashes, and reducing reuse so recovered secrets have less value.

beginner.definition: Passwords are often stored in a scrambled form called a hash. Password cracking means trying huge numbers of possible passwords, scrambling each one the same way and seeing which result matches. The match reveals the original password.
beginner.whyItMatters: If an attacker steals the stored hashes, they can work on them quietly on their own computers. Your systems see nothing, because the attempts happen far away from your network. A cracked password may open other systems where the same password is reused. It also defeats protections that stop attackers from logging in with the hash itself.
howItWorks: The attacker first steals password hashes from a system or a device configuration store.
They copy the hashes to their own hardware, away from the victim network.
A program scrambles each word from a long candidate list in the same way.
Each result is compared with the stolen hash until one matches, revealing the password.
Rules and lists from real breach data make common human choices far quicker to guess.
Precomputed tables answer lookups instantly when the hash type and length allow it.
beginner.example: A thief steals a sealed envelope from an office and takes it home. Inside are the door keys, but each key is blank. At home the thief has a machine that cuts thousands of key shapes and tests each one against the lock pattern on paper. The office never sees the attempts, and simply changes every lock once the theft is known.
takeaways: Cracking happens off site, so your logs will not show the guessing at all.
Protect the hash stores themselves: that is where defenders can still intervene.
Stop password reuse, because one cracked hash can open many unrelated systems.

objectives: Explain how password cracking recovers plaintext from stolen password hashes.
Distinguish offline cracking from online password guessing in both method and evidence.
Describe the common sources of hashes, including host credential stores and device configuration data.
Explain why cracking activity cannot be observed in victim authentication logs.
Outline defensive actions that reduce the value of a stolen hash, such as removing reuse.
